docs.explain:
Three functions cover most date work. TODAY returns the current day, DATEDIF measures a distance in whole units, and EOMONTH lands on the last day of a month. Each returns a serial, so each can feed the next formula.

The first screen ages a policy opened in January 2022 against a clock pinned to 15 March 2024, and asks for whole months: DATEDIF stops at 26. The second pays an invoice dated 1 March on the last day of the following month, which is 30 April, serial 45412. EOMONTH's second argument is a month offset, not a unit.

Keep the offset and the unit apart: EOMONTH's 1 moves one month forward and DATEDIF's "M" counts whole months. A wrong offset still returns a date and a wrong unit still returns a number, so compare the answer with the calendar.

errors.text: DATEDIF was given an end date before its start date, which leaves no positive interval to count.
EOMONTH was asked for an offset that lands outside the range of serials, such as a date before 1900.
A date argument arrived as text that cannot be read as a date, which leaves no serial underneath it.

seo.title: TODAY, DATEDIF and EOMONTH in Excel
seo.description: TODAY says what day it is, DATEDIF counts completed months up to it, and EOMONTH finds the edge of a month. The offset and the unit are not the same thing.
